s1.syndrome_frame: Acute onset of psychotic symptoms with hallucinations and delusions in a previously healthy individual
salient_findings: Episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, and grandiose and persecutory delusions
key_facts: 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history
1-week history of escalating behavioral changes
Family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, and hallucinations
Denies head injury, substance use, or stressors
No family history of psychiatric illness
Potential mercury exposure through work in a mining community
No systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19
Afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
General and neurologic exams were unremarkable
Elevated γ‐glutamyl transferase at 81 IU/L
Total bilirubin 26 μmol/L
Malaria and typhoid screens were negative
Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat
Head CT scan was normal
Lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive

shortlist.label: COVID-19 Psychosis
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis and presents with acute onset of psychotic symptoms

shortlist.label: Mercury Poisoning
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has potential mercury exposure through work in a mining community and presents with psychotic symptoms

shortlist.label: Schizophrenia
shortlist.why_kept: Patient presents with hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, which are characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia

shortlist.label: Autoimmune Encephalitis
shortlist.why_kept: Patient presents with acute onset of psychotic symptoms and has a normal head CT scan, which may suggest an autoimmune cause

shortlist.label: N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptor Encephalitis
shortlist.why_kept: Patient presents with acute onset of psychotic symptoms, hallucinations, and delusions, which are characteristic symptoms of this condition

raw.rationale: The patient's acute onset of psychiatric symptoms, including hallucinations and delusions, in the context of a confirmed COVID-19 infection, supports this diagnosis. The absence of prior psychiatric history and the temporal relationship between the COVID-19 infection and the psychiatric symptoms further strengthen this choice.

rejected.label: Mercury Poisoning
rejected.why: While the patient has potential mercury exposure, there are no specific symptoms or lab findings indicative of mercury poisoning, such as tremors, kidney damage, or specific patterns of cognitive impairment.

rejected.label: Schizophrenia
rejected.why: The acute onset of symptoms over one week is atypical for schizophrenia, which usually has a more gradual onset. Additionally, the presence of a confirmed COVID-19 infection provides a more immediate explanation for the psychiatric symptoms.

rejected.label: Autoimmune Encephalitis
rejected.why: There is no specific evidence provided for an autoimmune cause, such as specific antibodies or inflammatory changes on the head CT scan, which would be expected in autoimmune encephalitis.

rejected.label: N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptor Encephalitis
rejected.why: Similar to autoimmune encephalitis, there is no specific evidence for NMDA receptor antibodies or the characteristic symptoms such as seizures, decreased level of consciousness, or distinctive movement disorders.
